attributes.body:
Being slightly more direct than てくれる, てもらう removes the meaning of 'to bestow' (to the speaker), and focuses on the meaning of 'to receive' (from the giver). With てもらう, に will mark the person that 'did something' for the subject, while が (or は) will highlight the receiver themselves.

In English, this grammar structure is regularly translated as 'to have (someone) do (A) for you', or 'to get (someone) to do (A) for you'. Literally, it means 'to receive the action of (A)'.

てもらう is also regularly used when receiving a service from someone, as てくれる would imply that the action was a favor.

attributes.description: How to use （〜して）あげる + くれる + もらう
When to use てもらう
てあげる vs てくれる vs てもらう

attributes.body: Both use the て form to talk about favors, but with different perspectives. てあげる focuses on the giver (you or someone close to you) doing something for someone else. てもらう focuses on the receiver having something done for them. For example, ケンに教えてあげた ('I taught/told Ken.') vs. ケンに教えてもらった ('Ken taught me.').

attributes.body: もらう is a basic verb meaning 'to receive,' often used when the speaker or someone in their in-group receives something from someone outside the group. For example, プレゼントをもらった means 'I received a present.' When used as てもらう after a verb in the て form, it shows that the speaker received the benefit of an action, as in 日本語を教えてもらった ('I had someone teach me Japanese').

second_relatable.title: てもらう

attributes.body: Both express receiving a favor, but from different perspectives. With てくれる, the subject is the giver and they do something for you. With てもらう, the subject is the receiver and they get someone to do something. For example, ケンが教えてくれた frames the action as 'Ken taught/told me.', while ケンに教えてもらった frames it as 'I had Ken teach/tell me.'.

attributes.body: てもらう describes getting someone to do something for you, e.g. 教えてもらった ('I had them teach/tell me.'). ていただけませんか is a polite way to ask for such a favor, as in 教えていただけませんか？ ('Would you kindly teach/tell me?'). Both involve receiving help but differ in politeness and usage.
